banner.title: THE DSG MAPPING YOUR SETTINGS, R557: printed pp. 114-117 - the mapping doctrine, the chapter closing in a single round with the child flipped in the same commit: the head (the orthographic map as the architectural blueprint showing exact relative sizes for distance and direction; the separate map per elevation level with the stairways and well shafts hard to picture; the perspective alternative - detailed 3-D maps for multi-level settings, the book's grids photocopied); Basic Mapping Considerations (the effective map communicating the necessary information, often in a few minutes of pencil and scratch paper; the tools - the straightedge, compass, protractor, templates, the felt-tip and razor-point pens thicker than the grid); Perspective Mapping (the advantages - the 3-D nature, the clearer level positions, the visible inter-level connections; the costs - the raised staircases and platforms obscuring the areas behind, the cramped rear squares, the drawing time; the two starting techniques - the photocopy method with the personal-use permission and the enlarged copies, the tracing-paper method with the tape fastened to clear tape, never the page); Selecting a Grid (the overall-shape match - the square grids for castles and dungeons, the narrow for caverns; the occluded areas designed to need little detail - the empty room or solid rock behind the tall stairway; the important detail toward the front, the lower platforms front and the higher rear, the stage-set imagining); Selecting a Starting Point (the design started near the front with the large squares for the intricate areas, the entrance possibly far to the rear; the control square centered under the highest tower, lining up the levels - the photocopies held to the light, the pencil marks); Drawing the Map (the orthographic likeness with the not-true squares; the outer limit first, or the huge staircase or central atrium spanning levels); Mapping Symbols (the orthographic symbols translating directly - doors, trapdoors, curtains, furniture; the 3-D objects changed to portray vertically too; the printed symbols from simple to elaborate); Splitting the Grid (the altitude mimicry by cut and shifted pieces; the tracing method - the paper pulled down to the scaled height; the photocopy method - the cut-outs placed at the proper elevation, the 20-foot platform twice the 10-foot-square distance above the cut line); Horizon Lines (the horizontal orientation; the perpendicular verticals with the T-square or the 90-degree triangle); Geomorphic Mapping (the time problem and the unpredictable PCs; the same-shape sections with the standardized edge points abutting any neighbor - the tremendous combinations; the underground, city, and fortress suitability; the small-part sections with their several unused areas; the shapes - the easiest squares, the three-orientation triangles needing more, the many-position harder hexagons; the planned connections; the standardized symmetric locations - the exact center or the 1/3-in pairs; the 60 x 60-foot section with its one or two connections per side against the square-mile realm's six to eight; the 75% entry rule against the enclosing dead ends); and Using Geomorphs (the random generation of huge areas with the deliberate exceptions; the numbered geomorphs and the d3/d4/d6 placement rolls for which face is north; the placed section as normal setting - the matching edge connections proceeding unnoticed, the mismatches dead-ending; the variety and orientations hiding the revisited sections) - the round ending before the perspective grid plates, which are graphics and pin nothing.

The chapter ends after the using-geomorphs tail; the perspective grid plates pp. 118-120 are graphics and pin nothing, and the compiled tables open at p. 121. A CLEAN-READ ROUND. consts.comment: the splitting example scale: each square on the grid equals 10 feet
consts.name: dcjGridSquareFeet

consts.comment: the splitting example: the platform raised 20 feet above the main floor
consts.name: dcjPlatformExampleFeet

consts.comment: the small geomorph section: a 60 x 60-foot square per map section
consts.name: dcjGeomorphSectionFeet

consts.comment: the small-section connections: perhaps only one potential connection per side - the minimum
consts.name: dcjGeomorphSmallConnsMin

consts.comment: the small-section connections: no more than two potential connections per side - the maximum
consts.name: dcjGeomorphSmallConnsMax

consts.comment: the square-mile realm section connections: as many as six per side - the minimum
consts.name: dcjGeomorphLargeConnsMin

consts.comment: the square-mile realm section connections: as many as eight per side - the maximum
consts.name: dcjGeomorphLargeConnsMax

consts.comment: at least 75% of the possible connections on each geomorph should provide a means of entry into another map section
consts.name: dcjGeomorphEntryPct

bools.comment: the orthographic map - the typical top-view blueprint of corridors, rooms, and doorways showing exact relative sizes, useful for recording distance and direction
bools.name: dcjOrthoDefines

bools.comment: a separate orthographic map must be drawn for each elevation level; stairways and well shafts running through levels are hard to picture across the assortment
bools.name: dcjOrthoLevelSplit

bools.comment: the perspective alternative: 3-D maps for multi-level settings above or below ground, learning a few points and photocopying the book's grids
bools.name: dcjPerspectiveIntro

bools.comment: an effective map communicates the necessary information; often accomplished in a few minutes with pencil and scratch paper
bools.name: dcjEffectiveMap

bools.comment: the tools improve appearance and legibility: straightedge, compass, protractor, templates, and felt-tip or razor-point pens drawing slightly thicker than the grid
bools.name: dcjMappingTools

bools.comment: the perspective advantages: the 3-D nature conveyed realistically, each level's position relative to the others clearer, the inter-level connections easier to see
bools.name: dcjPerspective3D

bools.comment: the perspective costs: raised features (staircases, platforms, ramps) obscure the areas behind them, the rear squares cramp detail, and the map takes more time to draw
bools.name: dcjPerspectiveCosts

bools.comment: the reward: maps communicating much more than room size or which wall holds the door
bools.name: dcjPerspectiveReward

bools.comment: technique one: photocopies of the grid - one per floor with extras for careful work, enlarged copies helpful; the photocopying permission granted for personal use
bools.name: dcjStartPhotocopy

bools.comment: technique two: the tracing-paper tablet - grid portions traced and details drawn in, held by hand or taped; the tape fastened to clear tape on the grid pages, never the book page itself
bools.name: dcjStartTracing

bools.comment: select the grid matching the overall shape: the square grids for castles and dungeons, the longer narrower grids for caverns and walls
bools.name: dcjGridShapeMatch

bools.comment: design the occluded areas to need little detail: the large empty room or the solid rock directly behind the tall stairway
bools.name: dcjGridObscureDesign

bools.comment: the important detailed areas go toward the front of the grid; the lower platforms front and the higher rear - the stage-set imagining with the whole acting area visible
bools.name: dcjGridFrontDetail

bools.comment: start the design as close to the front as possible - the large front squares for the most intricate areas, though the entrance itself may lie far to the rear
bools.name: dcjStartFront

bools.comment: the control square: a single grid square roughly centered under the highest tower or the top level's midpoint, lining up the levels - photocopies held to the light, pencil marks on the traced copies
bools.name: dcjControlSquare

bools.comment: with the grid established, drawing a perspective map is much like an orthographic one - the biggest difference being the not-true squares of the grid
bools.name: dcjDrawLikeOrtho

bools.comment: draw the outer limit of the design first to visualize the structure and line up the levels - or start with the huge staircase or central atrium spanning several levels
bools.name: dcjDrawOuterFirst

bools.comment: orthographic symbols translate directly - doors, trapdoors, curtains, furniture - while the 3-D objects change slightly, portrayed vertically as well as horizontally
bools.name: dcjSymbolsTranslated

bools.comment: the 3-D symbols printed beside the grids - photocopy, trace, or cut and paste; styles from simple to elaborate, the familiarity developing quickly
bools.name: dcjSymbolStyles

bools.comment: mimic minor altitude changes by cutting the grid into pieces shifted up or down - especially for uneven underground environments
bools.name: dcjSplitGrid

bools.comment: the tracing method: the main floor grid drawn except the raised areas, the tracing paper pulled down until the area sits at the scaled height, the area drawn in its correct location; below-floor areas by moving the paper up
bools.name: dcjSplitTracing

bools.comment: the photocopy method: the raised areas cut from a copy, the rest glued to another sheet, the cut-outs placed at the proper elevation - the 20-foot platform twice the 10-foot-square distance above the cut line
bools.name: dcjSplitPhotocopy

bools.comment: each sample grid includes a horizon line; orient the grid so the horizon is horizontal to view it correctly
bools.name: dcjHorizonOrient

bools.comment: verticals drawn perpendicular to the horizon line - pillars, staircases, and ladders not toppling - with a T-square or a 90-degree triangle
bools.name: dcjHorizonVertical

bools.comment: the geomorphic problem: the DM lacks time to map every region the PCs may visit, and their actions are unpredictable - mapping only the immediate future is unreliable
bools.name: dcjGeomorphProblem

bools.comment: geomorphic maps: same shape and size, with standardized entry and exit points around the edges; any edge abuts a neighbor, yielding a tremendous number of combinations
bools.name: dcjGeomorphDefines

bools.comment: the geomorphic advantage: not mapping every square foot of a massive region - combinations of geomorphs create the needed areas; well-suited to underground settings, large cities, and sprawling fortresses
bools.name: dcjGeomorphSuitable

bools.comment: a single geomorphic section portrays only a small part of the setting, assembled like puzzle pieces - and a block may contain several separate adventure areas, of which you need not use all
bools.name: dcjGeomorphSections

bools.comment: the shapes: squares, equilateral triangles, or hexagons - squares easiest, triangles limited to three orientations (needing more geomorphs), hexagons with the most positions but harder to draw; the square combines the best features
bools.name: dcjGeomorphShapes

bools.comment: plan the possible connections between sections - plenty of route options without every connection leading through
bools.name: dcjGeomorphPlanConnections

bools.comment: the connections standardized and symmetric left-right: the exact center of each side or a pair each 1/3 of the distance in from the edge - measured carefully or the sections will not line up
bools.name: dcjGeomorphStandardized

bools.comment: with a collection of geomorphs, randomly generate areas of huge proportions - though a fitting section may be placed deliberately; the overall map generated by a few die rolls and varied placement
bools.name: dcjGeomorphRandom

bools.comment: the placement rolls: number the geomorphs and roll for the starting section; the positions equal the sides - the d3, d4, or d6 rolled to determine which face is north
bools.name: dcjGeomorphPositions

bools.comment: a placed geomorph is treated as a normal part of the setting map; at a section edge, roll a new geomorph and its orientation - matching connections proceed unnoticed, mismatches wander into a dead end and another path
bools.name: dcjGeomorphExplore

bools.comment: variety and many orientations create a huge region of well-mapped terrain - the players never knowing they pass through sections previously explored
bools.name: dcjGeomorphVariety

examples.note: the splitting example: 10-foot squares, the 20-foot platform.
the platform grid twice the square distance above the cut line.
the small geomorph: the 60 x 60-foot section.
the small-section connections: one, perhaps two, per side.
the square-mile realm: six to eight connections per side.
the entry rule: at least 75% of connections providing entry.
the geomorphs: the shapes and the standardized connections.
the craft: the perpendicular verticals and the control square.
